title: Circuit Breakers Stop Cascades ⚡
ig_caption:
A service dies… who goes down with it? 👀
Circuit Breakers = fail fast + self-heal.

• 0 FAILED REQUESTS → when the upstream starts failing, the breaker prevents new traffic from piling on
• ~80ms AVG LATENCY → requests are cut off quickly so clients don’t sit and retry endlessly
• Self-healed ✓ → after a cool-down, the breaker probes recovery instead of assuming failure is permanent
• No breaker: failure spreads → cascading retries and resource exhaustion
• Breaker: fail fast, isolate blast radius → system stays responsive under stress

Production takeaway: Set circuit breaker thresholds around real SLOs (error rate/timeouts) and pair them with sane client retries/backoff.
Avoid “retry storms” by failing fast when dependencies degrade.

What’s your biggest real-world failure mode: slow timeouts, retry storms, or shared dependency outages?
fb_caption:
A dependency fails, and the real question is: will the failure stay contained—or will it cascade?

In the reel, the circuit breaker acts like an isolation boundary:

• During failure conditions, the system short-circuits calls to the unhealthy upstream.
• This drives “fail fast” behavior, turning many slow, doomed attempts into rapid rejection.
• The observed outcome is fewer failed requests and dramatically improved tail behavior (e.g., ~80ms average latency) because threads/connection pools aren’t consumed waiting on an already-broken dependency.

Architectural trade-offs:

• Reliability vs. Accuracy: Failing fast means some requests are rejected even if the upstream might recover mid-flight. That’s the point—protect the system’s overall health.
• Latency vs. Availability: With a breaker, you trade immediate success probability for preserved service responsiveness. Clients can handle the failure more predictably.
• Detection vs. Stability: Thresholds (error rate, consecutive failures, timeout rates) must balance sensitivity (stop cascades early) against flapping (breaking and restoring too aggressively).

Scalability & resilience considerations:

• Preventing cascading failures requires limiting resource amplification: retries, timeouts, and queued work.
• Circuit breakers complement bulkheads (thread/concurrency limits), timeouts, and jittered retries to ensure dependency failures don’t overwhelm shared infrastructure.
• Recovery strategy matters: use half-open probing with limited traffic to validate recovery before reopening the floodgates.

Practical best practice:

Tune circuit breaker settings to your SLOs and real traffic patterns, and verify behavior under chaos tests (dependency latency spikes, partial outages, intermittent 5xx). Combine with capped retries + exponential backoff to avoid retry storms.

Hot question for discussion: What are you seeing more often in production—cascades caused by retries, or cascades caused by connection/thread pool exhaustion?
